topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: A 5-mark compound-solid question in most series (November 2024 Q12, Summer 2023 Q13, Summer 2024 Q9) and a 6–7 mark cone-difference or proof question among the last three (November 2024 Q22, Summer 2023 Q23, Summer 2026 Q23). Together they are worth about 11 marks of the 100.
mustMemorise: Frustum volume = large cone − small cone; both radii and both heights are given, because similar shapes are excluded here
Compound solids: add or subtract volumes; for surface area count only the faces that touch the air
The flat ring where two cylinders meet is πR² − πr², a difference of areas, never π(R − r)²
Cylinder: V = πr²h and curved surface = 2πrh — neither is on the formula sheet
Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³ and curved surface = 2πr², both half the sphere versions
πrl uses the slant height; (1/3)πr²h uses the perpendicular height; l² = r² + h² links them
Bracket a scaled radius before squaring: (3r)² = 9r²
Keep full accuracy through the working and round once on the answer line
onFormulaSheet: Curved surface area of cone = πrl
Volume of prism = area of cross-section × length
notOnThisSpec: Using similar shapes to find the missing height or radius of a frustum — the Teacher Guidance on M4-GM-01 says frustum questions will not require knowledge of similar shapes, so both cones are always given
A single formula for the volume of a frustum (it is built from the cone formula, and is not on the sheet)
Surface area of a frustum requiring the slant height to be derived from similar triangles
Volumes of revolution or calculus methods (A level, not GCSE)

note.title: Frustums and compound solids
note.subject: maths

given: Curved surface area of cone = πrl
Volume of prism = area of cross-section × length
mustKnow: Area of a circle πr² and circumference 2πr
Volume of a cylinder πr²h and curved surface area 2πrh
Hemisphere: half the sphere formulae, so (2/3)πr³ and 2πr²
Pythagoras to link slant height and perpendicular height: l² = r² + h²

notOnThisSpec: Using similar shapes to find a frustum's missing dimensions (excluded by the Teacher Guidance on M4-GM-01)
Volumes of revolution (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Find the volume of a frustum as the difference of two cone volumes, with both cones given
Find the volume of a compound solid by adding or subtracting the volumes of its parts
List the external faces of a compound solid and calculate the total surface area, naming each area beside its calculation
Treat the contact ring between two stacked cylinders as πR² − πr²
Halve the sphere formulae correctly for a hemisphere, and use a diameter only after halving it
Choose the slant height for πrl and the perpendicular height for the volume, using Pythagoras if only one is given
Set up and solve an equation for an unknown radius, bracketing a scaled radius before squaring
Apply a percentage-fill or a 'how many containers' condition, and round the count the way the context demands
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). Two places in the paper. A 5-mark compound-solid item in the first half (November 2024 Q12 total surface area of two stacked cylinders, Summer 2023 Q13 a cylinder with an overlap, Summer 2024 Q9 a cylinder emptied into hemispherical cups), marked MA1 per named area or volume with a final A1; and a 6- to 7-mark item in the last five questions where a frustum or difference of cones is set up as an equation in an unknown radius (November 2024 Q22, Summer 2023 Q23, Summer 2026 Q23 as a proof). The second kind is where the A grades are decided.
traps: Counting the faces where two solids meet, or totalling the complete surface areas of both parts (November 2024 M4 Q12, November 2024 M3 Q26)
Calculating volumes when the question asks for surface area — a large number of candidates did (November 2024 M3 Q26)
Treating the contact ring as π(R − r)² instead of πR² − πr²
Squaring a scaled radius without the bracket: (3r)² written as 3r² (November 2024 M4 Q22, where almost nobody finished)
Using the whole sphere formula for a hemisphere, or ignoring a '90% full' condition (Summer 2024 M4 Q9)
Substituting a diameter where the formula wants a radius
Using the slant height in the volume formula, or the perpendicular height in πrl
Rounding each part before adding, instead of once at the end
Leaving calculations unlabelled when the question says show your working out clearly (November 2024 M4 Q12)

Adding a stated overlap on at the end as though it were extra area, or folding it into the radius before you start. An overlap adds to the distance the surface has to wrap, so correct that distance first, find the curved surface area from it, and leave the two circular ends out of the total (Summer 2023 M4 Q13)

Finding the cone's height, then its slant, then its circumference, and stopping there because the link back to the sector is never made: the sector's arc is the circumference of the cone's base and the sector's radius is the slant height, and the angle is the fraction of the full circle those two give (Summer 2023 M4 Q23)

noteBlocks.lede: Cut the top off a cone, parallel to its base, and the piece left is a frustum: a bucket, a lampshade, a paper cup. A compound solid joins shapes you already know, such as a dome on a cylinder. Volumes add or subtract; a surface area counts only the faces you could touch.
can: Find a frustum's volume as the large cone minus the small cone, each with its own radius and height.
Add or subtract volumes for a compound solid, and count only the faces that touch the air for its surface area.
Set a volume equal to an expression in r, bracket before squaring, and solve for the radius.

noteBlocks.caption: Take the dashed cone, radius r and height h, away from the whole cone, radius R and height H.

noteBlocks.text: A frustum is a cone minus a cone

noteBlocks.md: Slice a cone parallel to its base and the bottom piece is a frustum. The piece cut off is itself a cone, so the frustum's volume is the whole cone minus the small cone: $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi R^2 H - \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Each cone keeps its own radius and its own height, both heights measured to the same point.

noteBlocks.title: Where the specification stops
noteBlocks.md: CCEA's Teacher Guidance says frustum questions will not need similar shapes, so both radii and both heights are always given. There is no frustum formula to learn: the cone formula on the sheet, used twice, is all of it.

noteBlocks.stem: A frustum is made from a cone of radius 8 cm and height 18 cm by removing the cone of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. Find its volume.

steps.decision: Large cone minus small cone, each with its own radius and height. Writing the whole subtraction first shows the method before any number.
The large cone: 64 × 18 ÷ 3 = 384. Keeping π as a letter keeps the numbers exact.
The small cone, with its own radius 4 and its own height 9: 16 × 9 ÷ 3 = 48.
Subtract, then use the calculator once: rounding each cone first would move the answer.

noteBlocks.title: Volume of a Frustum
noteBlocks.why: The same subtraction on another frustum, at writing speed. Watch it after the steps above, then try the check without going back.

noteBlocks.prompt: A frustum is made from a cone of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm by removing the cone of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Which calculation gives its volume?
noteBlocks.explain: Large cone minus small cone, each with its own radius and height, as step 1 of See it set up the pot of radii 8 and 4. Here that is $144\pi - 18\pi = 126\pi$ cm³.

optionNotes.why: That subtracts the lengths first and builds one smaller cone. Volumes do not follow lengths: work out each cone, then subtract the volumes.
The small cone is the piece cut away, so its volume is taken off, not added.

twin.prompt: A frustum is made from a cone of radius 9 cm and height 15 cm by removing the cone of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. Which calculation gives its volume?
twin.explain: Large cone minus small cone: $405\pi - 15\pi = 390\pi$ cm³.

optionNotes.why: Subtracting the radii and the heights builds one smaller cone, not the frustum. Find both cones, then subtract.
Adding puts the removed cone back; the frustum is what is left after it is taken away.

noteBlocks.title: Lengths do not subtract
noteBlocks.md: Subtract the lengths instead, $8 - 4$ and $18 - 9$, and you build a cone of radius 4 and height 9: the small cone itself. A cone's volume multiplies its radius by itself and then by its height, so doubling both lengths makes the volume $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ times as big. Only whole volumes subtract.

noteBlocks.stem: Why does $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(8-4)^2(18-9)$ not give the frustum of the first See it?

steps.decision: Subtracting the lengths first builds one cone, of radius 4 and height 9.

steps.working: $48\pi$ is the small cone, not the frustum's $336\pi$
steps.decision: That cone is exactly the piece that was removed; the frustum holds seven times as much.
Doubling the radius and the height made the volume 8 times as big, not 2 times. Volume does not follow lengths, so only volumes subtract.

noteBlocks.prompt: A frustum comes from a cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm with the cone of radius 2 cm and height 3 cm removed. What is its volume?
noteBlocks.explain: Work out each cone, then subtract: $108\pi - 4\pi = 104\pi$. Subtracting the lengths builds one cone, $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(4)^2(6) = 32\pi$, far too small, as step 1 of See it found.

optionNotes.why: That is one cone of radius 6 − 2 and height 9 − 3. Lengths do not subtract: find 108π and 4π, then take one from the other.
108π + 4π adds the removed cone back on. The frustum is what is left: 108π − 4π.

twin.prompt: A frustum comes from a cone of radius 10 cm and height 12 cm with the cone of radius 5 cm and height 6 cm removed. What is its volume?

optionNotes.why: That is the removed cone alone; subtracting the lengths, 10 − 5 and 12 − 6, builds that same cone. The frustum is 400π − 50π.
Adding the small cone puts the removed piece back; subtract it instead.

noteBlocks.md: The sheet gives the sphere: $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ for its volume and $4\pi r^2$ for its surface. A hemisphere is half a sphere, so halve both. Its flat face is a circle, $\pi r^2$, and it counts only when it is on the outside of the solid.

noteBlocks.title: Sheet or memory?
noteBlocks.md:
**On the Higher sheet:** the cone, $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ and $\pi r l$; the sphere, $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and $4\pi r^2$; a prism; a trapezium.
**Must be known:** $\pi r^2$ and $2\pi r$; the cylinder, $\pi r^2 h$ and $2\pi r h$; a hemisphere, as halves of the sphere; a ring, $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$.

noteBlocks.stem: A solid hemisphere has radius 7 cm. Find its volume and its total surface area.

steps.decision: Halve the sphere's volume from the sheet; the same thing is often written ⅔πr³.
Halve the sphere's surface too. Using the whole sphere was a slip the Summer 2024 report named.

steps.working: flat face $= \pi(7)^2 = 49\pi$, so the total is $147\pi = 461.8$ cm²
steps.decision: A solid hemisphere has its flat circle on the outside; a dome glued onto another solid does not.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is printed on the Higher formula sheet?
options: Curved surface area of a cylinder
noteBlocks.explain: The sheet prints the cone and the sphere, and the See it halved the sphere's two formulas from it. Both cylinder formulas, $\pi r^2 h$ and $2\pi r h$, are yours to know.

optionNotes.why: Not printed: πr²h has to be known, as the must-know list says.

optionNotes.option: Curved surface area of a cylinder
optionNotes.why: Not printed: 2πrh has to be known. It is the unrolled rectangle, 2πr wide and h tall.

twin.prompt: Which of these must you know, because the Higher sheet does not print it?
options: Curved surface area of a cone
twin.explain: The sheet prints the sphere and the cone; the cylinder's $\pi r^2 h$ is yours to know.

optionNotes.why: Printed: 4/3 πr³ is on the sheet, and a hemisphere is half of it.

optionNotes.option: Curved surface area of a cone
optionNotes.why: Printed: πrl is on the sheet, with l the slant height.

noteBlocks.prompt: Curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius $r$?
noteBlocks.explain: Half the sphere's $4\pi r^2$, as step 2 of See it halved $4\pi(7)^2$. The flat circle, $\pi r^2$, is extra and counts only when it is on the outside.

twin.prompt: Volume of a hemisphere of radius $r$?

twin.explain: Half the sphere's $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, as step 1 of See it halved it.

noteBlocks.caption: Volume: the parts add, cylinder plus cone, each with its own height.

noteBlocks.md: Build the solid from shapes you know and add their volumes, each part with its own height. If a part is cut out or drilled away, subtract it instead. Two parts that meet usually share a radius, but never a height.

noteBlocks.stem: A cone of radius 5 cm and height 9 cm stands on a cylinder of radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find the volume of the solid.

steps.decision: The cylinder is not on the sheet: πr²h is recall. Its height is the 12 cm of the cylinder part only.
The cone shares the radius and has its own height, 9 cm.
Add the parts, then round once.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm stands on a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. What is the solid's volume, in cm³, to 1 decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: Cylinder $\pi(3)^2(10) = 90\pi$ plus cone $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(4) = 12\pi$ makes $102\pi = 320.4$ cm³, the parts added as step 3 of See it added them.

twin.prompt: A cone of radius 4 cm and height 6 cm stands on a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 5 cm. What is the solid's volume, in cm³, to 1 decimal place?

noteBlocks.text: Surface area: only the faces you can touch

noteBlocks.alt: A hemisphere sitting on a cylinder of the same radius. Labels point to the three outside faces: the curved dome, the curved side of the cylinder and the bottom circle. The circle where they meet is hidden inside.

noteBlocks.caption: Three faces touch the air. The two circles where the parts meet are sealed inside and never count.

noteBlocks.md: Surface area works differently. Count only the faces you could paint: where two solids meet, the two touching faces are sealed inside and neither counts. List the outside faces first, then work out each one with its name beside it.

noteBlocks.stem: A hemisphere of radius 8 cm sits on a cylinder of radius 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find the solid's total surface area.

steps.working: outside: the bottom circle, the curved side and the dome
steps.decision: List the faces before calculating. The cylinder's top and the dome's flat face are pressed together, so both are hidden.
Name each area as you work it out.
Unrolled, the side is a rectangle 2πr wide and h tall; 2πrh is not on the sheet.
Half the sphere's surface, from the sheet's 4πr².
Add the named areas and round once.

noteBlocks.prompt: A hemisphere of radius 2 cm sits on a cylinder of radius 2 cm and height 7 cm. Which sum is the solid's total surface area?
noteBlocks.explain: Three faces touch the air, as step 1 of See it listed: the bottom circle $\pi(2)^2$, the curved side $2\pi(2)(7)$ and the dome, half of $4\pi(2)^2$. The cylinder's top is sealed under the dome.

optionNotes.why: Starting with 2π(2)² counts both of the cylinder's circles, but its top is sealed under the dome; only the bottom circle is outside.
4π(2)² is a whole sphere. The dome is a hemisphere, so halve it: 2π(2)².

twin.prompt: A hemisphere of radius 9 cm sits on a cylinder of radius 9 cm and height 4 cm. Which sum is the solid's total surface area?
twin.explain: Bottom circle, curved side and dome: $81\pi + 72\pi + 162\pi = 315\pi$ cm².

optionNotes.why: 4π(9)² is the whole sphere; the dome is half of it, 2π(9)².
The bottom circle is missing. The solid stands on it, but it is still an outside face.

noteBlocks.prompt: A solid cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm has a hemisphere of radius 3 cm on top. How many separate areas are on the outside?
noteBlocks.explain: The bottom circle, the curved side and the dome, the three faces step 1 of See it listed. The cylinder's top circle and the hemisphere's flat face are pressed together, so neither is on the outside.

twin.prompt: Two hemispheres of the same radius are joined at their flat faces. How many separate areas are on the outside?
twin.explain: Two domes. The two flat faces are pressed together, so neither shows: the solid is a sphere, 4πr².

noteBlocks.caption: The shaded ring is πR² − πr²: a difference of two circles, never π(R − r)².

noteBlocks.md: Stand a narrow cylinder on a wide one and the wide cylinder's top is only partly covered. What shows is a ring, the big circle minus the small one: $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$. The narrow cylinder's bottom is hidden; its top circle is outside.

The marks follow the faces. In November 2024 a 5-mark stacked-cylinder question gave a mark for each area named beside its calculation and the last for the total; many candidates added both cylinders' complete surfaces instead.

noteBlocks.stem: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm stands centrally on a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 4 cm. Find the solid's total surface area.

steps.working: outside: bottom circle, wide side, ring, narrow side, top circle
steps.decision: Walk round the solid and list every face that touches the air before working any out.
The wide cylinder keeps its bottom circle and its curved side.
The ring is a difference of two circles, never π(7 − 3)².
The narrow cylinder keeps its curved side and its top circle; its bottom is sealed.
Add the five named areas and round once.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two cylinders of radii 9 cm and 5 cm are stacked, the narrow one on top. What is the area of the ring left showing?
noteBlocks.explain: The ring is the big circle minus the small one, as step 3 of See it took $\pi(3)^2$ from $\pi(7)^2$: $81\pi - 25\pi = 56\pi$ cm². A difference of areas is never the area of a difference.

optionNotes.why: That is one circle of radius 4, 16π, far smaller than the ring's 56π. Take the small circle's area from the big circle's.
That is a difference of circumferences, a length in cm; an area needs πr².

twin.prompt: Two cylinders of radii 11 cm and 6 cm are stacked, the narrow one on top. What is the area of the ring left showing?
twin.explain: Big circle minus small circle: $121\pi - 36\pi = 85\pi$ cm².

optionNotes.why: One circle of radius 5 is 25π, not the ring; subtract the areas, not the radii.
The small circle is covered, so its area is taken away, not added.

noteBlocks.prompt: A 5-mark question says “Calculate the total surface area. Show your working out clearly.” What earns the first four marks?
options: One mark for each external area, named beside its calculation
One mark for each formula quoted from the sheet
Four marks for the final total
noteBlocks.answer: One mark for each external area, named beside its calculation
noteBlocks.explain: The scheme follows the faces, as the November 2024 one did: a mark for each outside area worked out with its name, then the total. A bare total earns no method marks, and a formula copied from the sheet earns nothing by itself.

optionNotes.option: One mark for each formula quoted from the sheet
optionNotes.why: Quoting a formula earns nothing by itself; the marks are for each area worked out and named.

optionNotes.option: Four marks for the final total
optionNotes.why: The total earns the last mark only; the four before it are one for each named area.

twin.prompt: A question says “Calculate the total surface area. Show your working out clearly.” Your total is wrong, but every area is named and worked out. What have you earned?
options: The marks for the named areas
Nothing, since the total is wrong
Only the mark for the total
twin.answer: The marks for the named areas
twin.explain: Each named area earns its own mark, so a slip in the addition costs only the mark for the total.

optionNotes.option: Nothing, since the total is wrong
optionNotes.why: Method marks stand on their own: each area worked out and named keeps its mark.

optionNotes.option: Only the mark for the total
optionNotes.why: The total is the one mark lost here; the named areas still earn theirs.

noteBlocks.text: Working back to a missing length

noteBlocks.md: Some questions give the volume and ask for a length. Put everything you know into the formula and leave the unknown as a letter. Simplify to one number times the unknown, divide, and take any square root last: a radius is positive.

noteBlocks.stem: A cone has volume 600 cm³ and height 14 cm. Find its radius.

steps.decision: Everything known goes into the formula; the radius stays a letter.
Undo the third and the 14π by multiplying by 3 and dividing by 14π.
The square root comes last, and only the positive root is a radius.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cone has volume 250 cm³ and height 12 cm. What is its radius, in cm, to 1 decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2(12) = 4\pi r^2 = 250$, so $r^2 = 19.89$ and $r = 4.5$ cm, the root taken last as step 3 of See it took it.

twin.prompt: A cone has volume 300 cm³ and height 10 cm. What is its radius, in cm, to 1 decimal place?

noteBlocks.text: Radii written in terms of r

noteBlocks.md: The hardest frustum questions give the radii as $r$ and a multiple of $r$, and the volume as a number. Set large cone minus small cone equal to that volume. Keep the multiple in a bracket before squaring: $(2r)^2 = 4r^2$, because the 2 is squared as well as the $r$.
In November 2024 only 2% of candidates scored full marks on a 7-mark question of this kind; most squared $3r$ without its bracket.

noteBlocks.stem: A frustum is made from a cone of radius $2r$ cm and height 12 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ cm and height 6 cm. Its volume is $168\pi$ cm³. Find $r$.

steps.decision: Large cone minus small cone, set equal to the volume, with 2r kept in its bracket.

steps.working: $(2r)^2 = 4r^2$, so the large cone is $16\pi r^2$
steps.decision: The bracket squares the 2 as well as the r: 4 × 12 ÷ 3 = 16.
The small cone is 6 ÷ 3 = 2 lots of πr²; collect into one number times πr².
π cancels from both sides. Take the square root last; a radius is positive.

noteBlocks.explain: The bracket squares the 3 as well as the r, as step 2 of See it squared the 2 of 2r: that gives 9r², then 9 × 4 ÷ 3 = 12, so it is 12πr².
Divide both sides by $105\pi$: $r^2 = 9$. A radius is positive, so $r = 3$, the root taken last as in step 4 of See it.

noteBlocks.md: Stacked cylinders with "Show your working out clearly" (November 2024): name every area, the ring included. Cups filled to 90% from a flask (Summer 2024): halve the sphere, apply the 90%, then round the count down. A frustum with radii 3r and r (November 2024, 2% full marks): bracket before squaring.

Proofs come too: that a sphere and a cube with edge equal to its radius never have equal surfaces (Summer 2024, 7% success), or a height in terms of a diameter (Summer 2026). The last mark is often about units or accuracy: litres from cm³, or the rounding asked for.

noteBlocks.stem: A bucket is a frustum: a cone of radius 10 cm and height 24 cm with the cone of radius 5 cm and height 12 cm removed. It is filled to 75% of its capacity, then poured into cups of 280 cm³. How many cups can be filled completely?

steps.decision: Large cone minus small cone gives the full capacity first.
The percentage applies to the whole volume, once it is found.
Divide by one cup's volume.
Round down: the sixth cup would not be full, and the question asks for full cups.

noteBlocks.prompt: A tank holds 5000 cm³ and is 90% full. How many 350 cm³ bottles can be filled completely from it?
noteBlocks.explain: $0.9 \times 5000 = 4500$ and $4500 \div 350 = 12.86$. Only 12 bottles are full, so round down, as step 4 of See it did.

twin.prompt: A flask holds 2000 cm³ and is 70% full. How many 180 cm³ cups can be filled completely from it?

noteBlocks.md: A proof question gives no numbers. Write each area or volume in letters, set them equal as the question says, and simplify until the condition appears. Divide only by something that cannot be zero, such as $2\pi r$ for a real solid.

noteBlocks.stem: A solid cylinder has radius $r$ and height $h$. Show that its curved surface equals the area of its two ends together only when $h = r$.

steps.working: curved surface $= 2\pi r h$; two ends $= 2\pi r^2$
steps.decision: Write each area in letters: the side unrolls to 2πr by h, and each end is a circle.
Set the two equal, as the question asks.
Divide both sides by 2πr, which is not zero for a real cylinder.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cone's curved surface, $\pi r l$, is twice the area of its base, $\pi r^2$. What must be true?
noteBlocks.explain: $\pi r l = 2\pi r^2$; divide both sides by $\pi r$, as step 3 of See it divided by $2\pi r$: $l = 2r$.

optionNotes.why: That divides the wrong way round: πrl = 2πr² gives l = 2πr² ÷ πr = 2r.
Dividing 2πr² by πr cancels one r, leaving 2r; no r² remains.

twin.prompt: A cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ has the same curved surface as a sphere of radius $r$. What must be true?
twin.explain: $2\pi r h = 4\pi r^2$; divide both sides by $2\pi r$: $h = 2r$.

optionNotes.why: That would need 2πrh = 2πr², a hemisphere's curved surface; a whole sphere's surface is 4πr².
Divide 4πr² by 2πr, not by πr: the 2 cancels too, leaving 2r.

noteBlocks.caption: Unroll the tube: a rectangle as wide as the circumference, 2πr, and as tall as the cylinder, h.

noteBlocks.md: The cylinder's curved surface is not on the sheet, and it need not be learned blind. Cut the tube straight down its side and unroll it: it lies flat as a rectangle.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that the curved surface of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ is $2\pi r h$.

steps.working: one side of the rectangle $= h$
steps.decision: The cut runs straight down the side, so one edge is the cylinder's height.
That edge was wrapped once round the circular end, so it is the circumference.
A rectangle's area is one side times the other.

noteBlocks.title: Surface Area of a Cylinder
noteBlocks.why: The same unrolled rectangle, then whole cylinders worked through. Watch it after the steps above.

noteBlocks.prompt: A label is wrapped once round a tin of radius 3.5 cm and height 10 cm, with no overlap. How long is the label?
options: 38.5 cm, the area of the top
noteBlocks.explain: The label's length is the rectangle's side from step 2 of See it, the circumference: $2\pi(3.5) = 22.0$ cm. The tin's height, 10 cm, is the label's other side.

optionNotes.option: 38.5 cm, the area of the top
optionNotes.why: π(3.5)² is an area in cm²; the label wraps round the edge, so its length is the circumference, 2πr.
10 cm is how far the label runs up the tin; its length goes round, 2π(3.5) = 22.0 cm.

twin.prompt: A label is wrapped once round a tin of radius 2.5 cm and height 8 cm, with no overlap. How long is the label?
options: 19.6 cm, the area of the top
twin.explain: Once round the tin is the circumference: $2\pi(2.5) = 15.7$ cm.

optionNotes.option: 19.6 cm, the area of the top
optionNotes.why: π(2.5)² is the area of the lid, in cm²; the label's length is 2π(2.5).
The height is the label's width up the tin; its length is the circumference.

noteBlocks.md:
Find a frustum's volume as large cone minus small cone.
Halve the sphere for a hemisphere; add $\pi r^2$ only for a flat face that is outside.
Add volumes; for a surface, name only the faces that touch the air.
Work out the ring where two cylinders meet as $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$.
Bracket a multiple of $r$ before squaring, and take the root last.

Expect a compound-solid question of about 5 marks most series, and a 6 or 7 mark frustum or proof question among the last few. Write the plan line first, name each area beside its calculation, keep π or the full calculator value to the end, and round once, to the accuracy asked; round a count down when every container must be full.

workedExamples.stem:
A plant pot is a frustum. It is made from a cone of base radius 12 cm and perpendicular height 24 cm by removing the cone of radius 5 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm from the top.

Calculate the volume of the plant pot. Give your answer correct to the nearest cubic centimetre.

steps.working: Volume of frustum = volume of large cone − volume of small cone
steps.decision: A frustum is a cone with its point cut off. Nothing else is needed: the Teacher Guidance says frustum questions will not require similar shapes, so both radii and both heights are always given.

options: Because the piece removed from the top is itself a cone
Because a frustum is half a cone
Because the volume of a frustum is on the formula sheet
whyMenu.explain: Cutting parallel to the base leaves a small cone on top. Subtract it. There is no frustum formula on the CCEA sheet: you build it from the cone formula, which is given.

steps.decision: The cone formula is on the Higher formula sheet. Write the substitution before the number so a marker can see the method, and keep the full calculator value.
Same formula, the removed cone's own radius and height. The 10 cm is the small cone's height, not the height of the pot.

steps.working: $3619.1 - 261.8 = 3357.3$ cm³, so the volume is $3357$ cm³
steps.decision: Subtract, then round once at the very end. Rounding each cone first would shift the answer; the general marking advice credits the most accurate figure seen.

options: Because rounding twice moves the final answer
Because the calculator only stores three figures
Because volumes must always be whole numbers
whyMenu.explain: Each rounding introduces an error that the subtraction keeps. Round once, on the answer line.

workedExamples.stem:
A hemisphere of radius 5 cm is fixed on top of a cylinder of radius 5 cm and height 14 cm.

Calculate the solid's total surface area, correct to 1 decimal place.

figure.alt: A hemisphere sitting on top of a cylinder of the same radius. The radius is labelled 5 cm on the base and the cylinder's height is labelled 14 cm.

steps.working: Faces that touch the air: bottom circle, curved side of the cylinder, curved surface of the hemisphere
steps.decision: List them before calculating anything. The cylinder's top circle is covered by the hemisphere's flat face, so neither of those two surfaces is on the outside. This list is where the examiners say the marks are won or lost.

options: Because surface area only counts surfaces you could paint
Because a hemisphere has no flat face
Because the top circle is smaller than the bottom circle
whyMenu.explain: The two faces meet and seal each other in. Counting them adds two circles that no paint could ever reach.

accepted: bottom circle, curved side of the cylinder, curved surface of the hemisphere

steps.decision: Label every calculation as you go. In November 2024 the examiners asked specifically for working laid out with each area named.
The cylinder is not on the formula sheet: $2\pi r h$ has to be known. It is the rectangle you get by unrolling the tube, with width equal to the circumference.
The sheet gives the sphere's surface area $4\pi r^2$; a hemisphere is half of it. Forgetting to halve is the error the Summer 2024 report named.
Add the three labelled areas and round once. In exact form this is $215\pi$ cm², which is a quick check: $215 \times \pi = 675.4$.

workedExamples.stem:
A container is a frustum made from a cone of base radius $4r$ cm and height 20 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ cm and height 5 cm from the top. The volume of the container is $420\pi$ cm³.

Find the value of $r$.

steps.decision: Set up the subtraction as an equation before simplifying anything. Each cone keeps its own radius and height, and $4r$ goes inside a bracket.
The bracket squares the 4 as well as the $r$. This one line is what the November 2024 examiners said almost every candidate lost: $3r$ was squared without brackets.

options: Because squaring $4r$ squares both the 4 and the $r$
Because the bracket can be ignored when the power is 2
whyMenu.explain: $(4r)^2 = 4r \times 4r = 16r^2$. Writing $4r^2$ squares only the letter and makes the answer four times too small.

steps.decision: Simplify each term separately: $16r^2 \times 20 = 320r^2$ and $r^2 \times 5 = 5r^2$, then $(320 - 5) \div 3 = 105$.
The $\pi$ cancels because the volume was given in terms of $\pi$. Take the positive square root only: a radius cannot be negative.

twin.stem: A funnel is a frustum made from a cone of base radius $3r$ cm and height 18 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ cm and height 6 cm. Its volume is $416\pi$ cm³. Find the value of $r$.

items.stem: How do you find the volume of a frustum?
items.skill: Know that a frustum is a difference of two cones

options.feedback: Cutting the top off parallel to the base leaves a smaller cone, so subtract its volume.
Adding puts the removed piece back. The frustum is what is left after the small cone is taken away.

options.text: Cone with the two radii subtracted first
options.feedback: Radii cannot be subtracted and then used in one cone formula: volume is not proportional to radius. Work out each cone and subtract the volumes.
The piece removed is only half the height in special cases, and even then the volumes are not halved: volume depends on the cube of the scale factor.

items.stem: A solid cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm stands on a wider cylinder. Which surfaces of the small cylinder are on the outside?
items.skill: Decide which faces of a compound solid touch the air

options.text: Its curved surface and its top circle
options.feedback: Its bottom circle is pressed against the wide cylinder, so it cannot be painted.

options.text: Its curved surface and both circles
options.feedback: The bottom circle is hidden where the two cylinders meet; counting it adds a face that no paint could reach.
The top circle is exposed. Curved surface only is what a question asks for when it says 'curved surface area'.

options.text: Its curved surface, its top circle and its bottom circle minus the wide circle
options.feedback: The ring belongs to the wide cylinder's top face, not to the small one. Assign each surface to one solid and count it once.

items.stem: Two cylinders of radii 10 cm and 4 cm are stacked. What is the area of the flat ring where the wide one is not covered?
items.skill: See the contact ring as a difference of two circles

options.feedback: The visible part of the wide top face is the large circle with the small circle taken out.
The radii were subtracted before squaring. $\pi(6)^2$ is a circle of radius 6, which is not the ring.
Those are circumferences, which are lengths. An area needs $\pi r^2$.
That is the whole top face. The middle is covered by the narrow cylinder and must be subtracted.

items.stem: What is the curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius 6 cm?

options.feedback: Half of $4\pi r^2$. The flat circle is separate and is only counted if it is on the outside.
That is the whole sphere. A hemisphere is half of it.
That is the volume formula, and the units give it away: cm³, not cm².
The flat circle has been included. It counts only when the flat face is exposed, which it is not when the hemisphere sits on something.

items.stem: A cone has base diameter 14 cm and height 24 cm. Which substitution gives its volume?
items.skill: Use the radius, not the diameter, in a formula

options.feedback: Halve the diameter first: $r = 7$.
The diameter was used as the radius, which makes the volume four times too big.
The height was halved as well. Only the diameter needs halving; 24 cm is already the perpendicular height.
That is a cylinder. A cone of the same base and height is one third of it.

items.stem: In a frustum problem the volume gives $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(3r)^2(15)$. What is this in terms of $r^2$?
items.skill: Bracket a scaled radius before squaring

options.feedback: $3r$ was squared as $3r^2$, so only the letter was squared. $(3r)^2 = 9r^2$.
The one third has been left out: $9 \times 15 = 135$, and that still has to be divided by 3.
The height has been dropped. Multiply by 15 as well, then divide by 3.

items.stem: A jug holds 2400 cm³ and is filled to 85% of its capacity. How much liquid is in it?

options.feedback: The 85% condition has been ignored. The capacity is not the amount poured in.
That is the empty space, 15% of the jug. The question asks for the liquid.
The volume has been divided by 0.85 instead of multiplied. Filling it partly gives less than the capacity, not more.

items.stem: A frustum is made from a cone of radius 12 cm and height 16 cm by removing the cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Which calculation gives its volume?
items.skill: A frustum is a difference of two cones

options.feedback: Large cone minus small cone, each with its own radius and height.
That subtracts the lengths first and builds one cone. Work out both cones, then subtract the volumes.
Adding puts the removed cone back; the frustum is what is left after it is taken away.

items.stem: A hemisphere of radius 6 cm sits on a cylinder of radius 6 cm. Which faces make the solid's total surface area?
items.skill: Only the faces that touch the air

options.text: The bottom circle, the curved side and the dome
options.feedback: The cylinder's top and the dome's flat face are pressed together, so neither is outside.

options.text: Both circles of the cylinder, the curved side and the dome
options.feedback: The top circle is sealed under the dome; only the bottom circle is outside.

options.text: The bottom circle, the curved side and a whole sphere
options.feedback: The dome is half a sphere, so its curved surface is half of 4πr².

items.stem: Two cylinders of radii 8 cm and 2 cm are stacked, the narrow one on top. What is the area of the ring left showing?
items.skill: The ring is a difference of circles

options.feedback: π(8)² − π(2)² = 64π − 4π = 60π: the big circle minus the small one.
That is π(8 − 2)², one circle of radius 6. Subtract the areas, not the radii.
2π(8) − 2π(2) is a difference of circumferences, a length; an area needs πr².

items.stem: In a frustum question the volume gives $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(4r)^2(6)$. What is this in terms of $r^2$?

options.feedback: Only the r was squared. The bracket squares the 4 too: (4r)² = 16r².
The one third was left out: 16 × 6 = 96, then divide by 3.

items.stem: A flask holds 3000 cm³ and is 80% full. How many cups of 350 cm³ can be filled completely from it?
items.skill: Apply the fill, then round a count down

options.feedback: 6.86 rounds to 7, but the seventh cup would not be full; round a count of full cups down.
3000 ÷ 350 = 8.57 uses the whole flask; only 80% of it holds water.

items.stem: A cone has volume 400 cm³ and height 12 cm. What is its radius?
items.skill: Work back to a radius, root last

options.feedback: 4πr² = 400, so r² = 31.8 and r = 5.64 cm.
That is r². The last step is the square root: r = 5.64 cm.
The one third was left out of the cone formula: (1/3)πr²(12) = 4πr², not 12πr².

context.setting: A plain solid cone, no context

parts.stem: Calculate the volume of a cone of base radius 6 cm and perpendicular height 15 cm. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: The cone formula is on the Higher formula sheet.
Square the radius before multiplying by the height.
parts.workedSolution: $V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi (6)^2 (15) = 565.5$ cm³, which is $565$ cm³ to 3 significant figures (exactly $180\pi$).

commonErrors.feedback: The one third has been left out, so that is a cylinder. A cone of the same base and height is a third of the cylinder.

context.setting: A plain solid hemisphere, no context

parts.stem: Calculate the volume of a hemisphere of radius 9 cm. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: The sphere volume is on the formula sheet.
Halve it for a hemisphere.
parts.workedSolution:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi (9)^3$$
$$= \tfrac{2}{3}\pi (729)$$
$$= 1526.8$$
 cm³, so $1530$ cm³ to 3 significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole sphere was used. A hemisphere is half of it, so halve the sphere formula before you substitute.

context.setting: A plain cone, no context

parts.stem: A cone has base radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. Calculate its curved surface area, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Curved surface area of a cone is on the formula sheet as πrl.
l is the slant height, not the perpendicular height.
parts.workedSolution: $\pi r l = \pi (7)(25) = 549.8$ cm², so $550$ cm² to 3 significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: The base circle has been added. 'Curved surface area' means the sloping surface only; the base is included only when the question says total surface area.

context.setting: A plain solid cone, no context

parts.stem: A solid cone has base radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm. Calculate its total surface area, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Total means curved surface plus base.
πrl is on the sheet; πr² is not, and must be known.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the curved surface only. A solid cone also has its base circle on the outside, so add πr².

context.setting: A frustum given as a large cone with a small cone removed

parts.stem: A frustum is made from a cone of base radius 9 cm and height 24 cm by removing the cone of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm from the top. Calculate the volume of the frustum, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Work out the two cones separately.
The small cone has its own height, 8 cm.
Subtract, then round once.
parts.workedSolution: Large cone $= \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(9)^2(24) = 2035.8$ cm³. Small cone $= \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(8) = 75.4$ cm³. Frustum $= 1960.4$ cm³, so $1960$ cm³.

commonErrors.feedback: The radii and heights were subtracted first and one cone formula used. Volume does not scale like that; work out both cones and subtract the volumes.

context.setting: A frustum given as a large cone with a small cone removed

parts.stem: A frustum is made from a cone of base radius 10 cm and height 30 cm by removing the cone of radius 4 cm and height 12 cm. Calculate the volume of the frustum, correct to the nearest cubic centimetre.
hints: Two cone calculations, then one subtraction.
Keep the full accuracy until the last line.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the large cone on its own, which is the first mark. The frustum is what is left after the small cone is subtracted.

context.setting: A cylinder with a hemisphere on top

parts.stem: A hemisphere of radius 4 cm sits on top of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 11 cm. Calculate the solid's volume, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Volumes of a compound solid add.
The cylinder volume is not on the sheet: πr²h.
Halve the sphere volume.
parts.workedSolution: Cylinder $= \pi(4)^2(11) = 552.9$ cm³; hemisphere $= \tfrac{2}{3}\pi(4)^3 = 134.0$ cm³. Total $= 687.0$ cm³, so $687$ cm³.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole sphere was used. A hemisphere is half of it, so halve the sphere formula before you substitute.

context.setting: A cone standing on a cylinder

parts.stem: A cone of radius 6 cm and height 14 cm sits on top of a cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 20 cm. Calculate the solid's volume, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Two volumes, added.
The cone keeps its own height, 14 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The cone was treated as a cylinder. Multiply the cone's πr²h by one third.

context.setting: Two stacked cylinders

parts.stem:
An ornament is a cone of radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm standing point downwards, with a hemisphere of radius 5 cm resting on its circular top.

expectedOrder: external faces are the curved surface of the cone and the curved surface of the hemisphere

scheme.for: states that the cone's base circle and the hemisphere's flat face are not on the outside

scheme.examinerNote: The line before the printed result must be seen; writing 115π with no supporting areas earns nothing.

hints: Which two surfaces could you paint?
πrl is on the formula sheet and uses the slant height.
Keep everything in terms of π so the printed answer appears.
parts.workedSolution: The cone's circular top is covered by the hemisphere's flat face, so the outside is the cone's curved surface and the hemisphere's curved surface. Cone: $\pi r l = \pi(5)(13) = 65\pi$. Hemisphere: $\tfrac{1}{2}(4\pi r^2) = 2\pi(5)^2 = 50\pi$. Total $= 65\pi + 50\pi = 115\pi$ cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The cone's base circle (25π) and the hemisphere's flat face (25π) have both been added, but they are pressed together and sealed in. Only the two curved surfaces are on the outside.
The perpendicular height was used in πrl. That formula needs the slant height, here 13 cm, which is the sloping distance from the rim to the point.

Halve the sphere volume for the hemisphere.
Add, then round once.

commonErrors.feedback: The slant height, 13 cm, was used in the volume formula. Volume uses the perpendicular height, 12 cm; the slant height belongs to πrl only.

parts.stem:
A bin is a frustum. It is made from a cone of radius $3r$ cm and perpendicular height 21 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ cm and perpendicular height 7 cm.

The volume of the bin is 1400 cm³. Calculate the diameter of the top of the bin, correct to 2 decimal places.

scheme.examinerNote: Giving 2.71 or 5.42 scores 6 of 7: the top radius is 3r, so the diameter is 6r.

hints: Write the subtraction of the two cone volumes as an equation equal to 1400.
Put 3r in a bracket before you square it.
Collect the r-squared terms, then divide.
The top radius is 3r, so the diameter is twice that.
parts.workedSolution: $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi (3r)^2 (21) - \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 (7) = 1400$. Since $(3r)^2 = 9r^2$, this is $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi(189r^2 - 7r^2) = \tfrac{182}{3}\pi r^2 = 1400$. So $r^2 = \dfrac{1400 \times 3}{182\pi} = 7.35$ and $r = 2.71$. The top radius is $3r$, so the diameter is $6r = 16.26$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: $(3r)^2$ is $9r^2$, not $3r^2$: squaring a bracket squares the number too. The method mark for the subtraction stands, but every line after this is three times too small. This is the step the November 2024 examiners said stopped almost everyone.
Six of the seven marks are earned: $r = 2.71$ is correct. The question asks for the diameter of the top, and the top radius is $3r$, so the diameter is $6r = 16.26$ cm.

The cylinder's top circle is covered by the hemisphere's flat face.
The hemisphere's curved surface is half of 4πr².

A whole sphere's surface was used for the dome. The hemisphere's curved surface is half of 4πr², so 2π(6.5)².

parts.stem: A bowl is a frustum. It is made from a cone of radius $5r$ cm and perpendicular height 20 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. The volume of the bowl is 5000 cm³. Calculate the diameter of the wider end of the bowl, correct to 1 decimal place.

So $r^2 = \dfrac{15000}{496\pi} = 9.63$ and $r = 3.10$. The wider end has radius $5r$, so its diameter is $10r = 31.0$ cm.

findTheMistake.stem: Eabha was asked for the total surface area of a solid made from a cylinder of radius 9 cm and height 7 cm with a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 6 cm on top. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Both cylinders were given their complete surface areas, so the two circles where they meet were counted even though they are sealed inside the solid. The wide cylinder contributes its bottom circle and the ring that is left uncovered, not two whole circles.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two method marks stand: both curved surfaces are right. The habit that fixes this is to list the faces that touch the air before any button is pressed, and to write the name beside each calculation. November 2024 M4 Q12: only the strongest candidates finished, and the examiners asked for exactly that layout.

findTheMistake.stem: Rory was asked to find $r$ for a frustum made from a cone of radius $4r$ and height 18 cm by removing the cone of radius $r$ and height 4.5 cm, with volume $282\pi$ cm³. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: $(4r)^2$ was written as $4r^2$, so only the letter was squared. Squaring the bracket squares the 4 as well: $(4r)^2 = 16r^2$, which makes the first term four times larger.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark for subtracting the two cone volumes is earned, and the algebra afterwards is handled cleanly. The single line that costs the rest is the missing bracket. Write $(4r)^2$ with the bracket, say “four squared is sixteen”, then substitute. November 2024 M4 Q22: almost nobody finished, and this was the reason the examiners gave.

findTheMistake.stem: Daniel was asked how many cups of radius 4 cm, shaped as hemispheres and filled to 90% of capacity, could be poured from a cylindrical flask of radius 5 cm and height 22 cm. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The whole sphere formula was used for a cup that is a hemisphere, and the 90% fill was never applied. Each cup holds half a sphere, and then only nine tenths of that.
findTheMistake.feedback: The flask volume is right and earns its mark. Two conditions in the stem were then passed over: hemisphere, and 90% full. Underline the words that change a number before you start, and check the size of the answer against them — smaller cups must give more cups, not fewer. Summer 2024 M4 Q9 lost marks for the same two reasons.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the volume of a frustum?
prompts.answer: Large cone minus small cone; each keeps its own radius and height.

prompts.prompt: Cylinders of radii $R$ and $r$ are stacked. What area shows on the wider top?
prompts.answer: The ring $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$: two circles subtracted.

prompts.prompt: What is the volume of a hemisphere of radius $r$?
What is the volume of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$?
prompts.answer: $\pi r^2 h$; you must know it, as the sheet omits it.

prompts.prompt: In a frustum question the radius is $3r$. What is $(3r)^2$?
prompts.answer: $9r^2$: the bracket squares the 3 as well.

prompts.prompt: Which height goes in the cone's curved surface, $\pi r l$?
prompts.answer: The slant height l, never the perpendicular height.

prompts.prompt: A division gives 7.8 containers. How many can be filled completely?
prompts.answer: 7: round down, since the eighth is not full.

prompts.prompt: Two solids are glued together. Do the touching faces count in the surface area?
prompts.answer: No: they are sealed inside, so neither face counts.

findings.asked: Total surface area of a solid made of two cylinders stacked.
findings.wentWrong: Only the strongest finished; errors included finding volume, forgetting to subtract the small circle where the cylinders meet, and using the wrong curved-surface formula. Examiners asked for work laid out with each calculation named.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Listed the external faces: two curved surfaces, the top circle, the bottom circle, and the ring (large circle minus small circle) where they join.
findings.rule: Count only surfaces that touch the air, and label each one.

findings.asked: The same compound surface area on M3.
findings.wentWrong: Many totalled the complete surface areas of both cylinders; others could not see the middle ring as a difference of circles; a large number calculated volumes instead.
findings.rule: The contact ring is the difference of two circles.

findings.asked: Find a cone's radius from the volume of a frustum-like difference of cones.
findings.wentWrong: Almost nobody finished: the subtraction of volumes was set up by some, but 3r was squared without brackets and the simplification failed.
findings.rule: Bracket (3r) before squaring; simplify each term separately.

insight.ruleToRemember: List the external faces of a compound solid one by one (the contact ring is a difference of two circles), label each calculation, and bracket scaled radii before squaring.
insight.aStarSignal: A frustum or stacked-solid problem set up as an equation in an unknown radius and solved without bracket errors.
